agrigento.intro: Agrigento's oldest trees grow among its temples. In the Valley of the Temples, olives estimated at around five centuries stand beside the temples of Juno and Concordia, one with a root running toward each. The FAI's Kolymbethra garden holds the widest olive in the town's register and a myrtle grown to seven and a half metres, and a carob four metres round stands by the ruins of the Temple of Olympian Zeus. Up in the town, two Moreton Bay figs shade Piazza Aldo Moro for free.
agrigento.meta_description: Agrigento's remarkable trees: olives of about 500 years beside the temples of Juno and Concordia, a giant myrtle, a temple carob and the town's figs.
agrigento.question_meta: Agrigento's oldest trees are olives in the Valley of the Temples, estimated at 500 to 600 years. Where they stand and how sure anyone is.
agrigento.question_answer: Agrigento's oldest trees are the olives of the Valley of the Temples. The olive registered at the Temple of Concordia is estimated at 500 to 600 years in the Sicilian region's tourist mapping, and the olive beside the path to the Temple of Juno at about 500 by the Italian Botanical Heritage guide. Both are estimates; nobody has cored either tree.
agrigento.question_context: Nearly every old tree in Agrigento stands inside the archaeological park, which means a ticket and a walk along the ridge of temples. The two olives with ages both come from single sources. The regional tourist mapping gives the olives at the Temple of Concordia 500 to 600 years, and the registered one there is actually the smaller of two; an unlisted olive 5.2 metres round grows about 45 metres away. The Italian Botanical Heritage guide gives about 500 years for the spiral-trunked olive on the path to the Temple of Juno, and notes that one of its roots runs toward each temple; blogs that call it a thousand years old give no basis. The widest olive in the register, 6.4 metres round and only five tall, grows in the FAI's Kolymbethra garden, which the same ticket covers, along with a myrtle that has reached 7.5 metres. Several of the park's trees have approximate pins and no recent photograph, and readers' pictures would settle them. Outside the park, two Moreton Bay figs on Piazza Aldo Moro are free and confirmed by visitors' records.

faq.q: How old is the olive tree at the Temple of Juno in Agrigento?
faq.a: About 500 years, according to the Italian Botanical Heritage guide. Blogs call it a thousand years old, but none gives a basis. Its trunk is 4.2 metres round and spirals clockwise, and one root runs toward the Temple of Juno and another toward the Temple of Concordia.

faq.q: Do I need a ticket to see Agrigento's old trees?
faq.a: For most of them, yes. The temple olives, the carob and the Kolymbethra garden trees are inside the Valley of the Temples archaeological park, which charges entry; a combined park and garden ticket was 20 EUR full price in 2026. The two figs on Piazza Aldo Moro in the town are free.

faq.q: What is the biggest olive tree in Agrigento?
faq.a: By the Sicilian register, the olive in the FAI's Kolymbethra garden, 6.4 metres round and about 5 metres tall. An olive on the Temple of Juno terrace measures 5.5 metres, and an unlisted olive at the Temple of Concordia 5.2.

palazzolo-acreide.intro: Palazzolo Acreide's town garden holds three trees on Italy's national register, all within a short walk. The Villa Comunale was laid out between 1877 and 1881 on the site of an old holm-oak wood, and a holm oak 5.65 metres round and 24 metres tall still stands in it, called the largest in Sicily by the naturalist association Natura Sicula. Beside it grow a cypress more than seven metres round and a cedar of Lebanon over a century old. Entry is free.
palazzolo-acreide.meta_description: Three registered giants in Palazzolo Acreide's free town garden: a holm oak called Sicily's largest, a 7-metre cypress and a century-old cedar of Lebanon.
palazzolo-acreide.question_meta: Palazzolo Acreide's biggest tree is a holm oak 5.65 metres round in the Villa Comunale, estimated at five to six centuries. Its rivals and its neighbours.
palazzolo-acreide.question_answer: Palazzolo Acreide's biggest tree is the holm oak of the Villa Comunale, 5.65 metres round and 24 metres tall. Natura Sicula, the naturalist association that measured it in 2015, calls it the largest holm oak in Sicily and estimates it at five to six centuries old. The garden is free and in the middle of town.
palazzolo-acreide.question_context: All three of the town's registered trees grow in one public garden, the Villa Comunale, built between 1877 and 1881 on land a local baron gave the town. The ground was once a holm-oak wood, and a few old oaks survive on the garden's south side. The biggest of them, 5.65 metres round and 24 metres tall, is the one Natura Sicula ranks as Sicily's largest holm oak, ahead of the Ilici di Carrinu on Etna, which they give at 5.15 metres; other people have measured the Etna trees differently, so the ranking is theirs. The cypress is the stranger tree. Cypresses grow tall rather than thick, and this one is more than seven metres round, which the association says no other cypress in the national register matches; they estimate it at about three centuries. The cedar of Lebanon is younger, over a century by the association's estimate. All three ages are estimates the association does not explain, and readers who know more are welcome to tell us. In November 2023 all three were reported in good health.

faq.q: Is the holm oak in Palazzolo Acreide the largest in Sicily?
faq.a: The naturalist association Natura Sicula says so, comparing its 5.65-metre girth with the 5.15 metres it gives the Ilici di Carrinu on Etna. Others have measured the Etna trees at different figures, so treat it as the association's ranking. The register confirms the 5.65 metres.

faq.q: How old are the trees in the Villa Comunale of Palazzolo Acreide?
faq.a: By Natura Sicula's estimates, the holm oak is five to six centuries old, the cypress about three centuries, and the cedar of Lebanon over a century. None of the three has a planting record or a core date.
Yes. It is the town's public garden, laid out between 1877 and 1881. We have not found published opening hours.

noto.intro: Noto's best-known tree once nearly lost its place to a view. A Norfolk Island pine 28 metres tall stands in the Villetta Ercole on Piazza XVI Maggio, beside Rosario Gagliardi's church of San Domenico, and a mayor once proposed moving it to clear the sightline. The culture minister refused, saying the tree was part of the landscape. It arrived at the end of the nineteenth century, bought from a travelling seller, and the region made it a monument of nature in 2005.
noto.meta_description: Noto's Norfolk Island pine: 28 metres tall beside San Domenico, bought from a travelling seller in the 1800s and saved from a mayor who wanted the view.
noto.question_meta: Noto's most remarkable tree is the Norfolk Island pine of the Villetta Ercole, beside San Domenico. How it got there and why it stayed.
noto.question_answer: Noto's most remarkable tree is the Norfolk Island pine in the Villetta Ercole on Piazza XVI Maggio, 28 metres tall by Sicily's register. It was bought from a travelling seller at the end of the nineteenth century, and it survived a mayor's plan to move it away from the front of San Domenico.
noto.question_context: The pine's story comes from a local culture site that cites Corrado Coppa's history of the town. The director of Noto's experimental winery bought two araucarias from a travelling seller at the end of the nineteenth century and kept them in pots beside the Casa Senatoria before they were planted in the Villetta Ercole, the small garden on Piazza XVI Maggio. One stands there today. When Noto's Late Baroque centre was being celebrated as World Heritage, the mayor proposed moving the whole tree to free the view of San Domenico, and the culture minister, Giuliano Urbani, answered that the tree was part of the landscape. Sicily's register gives it 28 metres and a girth of 3 metres and lists it for rarity and form as well as size; the culture site gives 32 metres and 3.5, and calls it once the largest Norfolk Island pine in Sicily and Italy. The region declared it a monument of nature in 2005, and Legambiente added a plaque in 2006. A 2025 photograph shows the crown visibly thin, and a care project funded by the ministry and the region is described.

faq.q: How tall is the Norfolk Island pine in Noto?
faq.a: Sicily's register of monumental trees gives 28 metres and a girth of 3 metres. A local culture site gives 32 metres and 3.5, and calls it once the largest of its kind in Sicily and Italy.

faq.q: Why was the Noto pine nearly moved?
faq.a: A mayor proposed digging it up, roots and all, to free the view of the church of San Domenico. The culture minister, Giuliano Urbani, answered that the tree was part of the landscape, and it stayed.
Yes. It is a public garden on Piazza XVI Maggio in the old town, and the pine can also be seen from the square.

ragusa.intro: Ragusa's biggest trees are not in the town but at Donnafugata Castle, about 20 kilometres away in the countryside. In the shaded first part of the castle park stand two Moreton Bay figs, about 25 metres apart, with trunks 9.5 and 9 metres round and crowns 25 metres high by Sicily's register of monumental trees. Other figs grow in the park, but none comes close. The park is a municipal visit with its own ticket.
ragusa.meta_description: Two Moreton Bay figs more than nine metres round in the park of Donnafugata Castle, about 20 km from Ragusa. Where they stand and how to visit.
ragusa.question_meta: Ragusa's biggest trees are two Moreton Bay figs at Donnafugata Castle, 9.5 and 9 metres round. Where to find them in the park.
ragusa.question_answer: The biggest trees near Ragusa are two Moreton Bay figs in the park of Donnafugata Castle, about 20 kilometres from the town. Sicily's register gives them trunks 9.5 and 9 metres round and a height of 25 metres. They stand about 25 metres apart in the shaded first part of the park.
ragusa.question_context: Donnafugata is a castle estate in the countryside south-west of Ragusa, and its park is visited with a municipal ticket; one source gives 4 EUR for the park alone and 10 EUR with the castle and museum, and hours differ between sources, so check with the Comune di Ragusa first. The Italian Botanical Heritage guide describes the first section of the park as shaded by large figs of this species, which older guides called Ficus magnolioides. Two of them are on Sicily's register of monumental trees, at 9.5 and 9 metres round and 25 metres tall, standing on buttress roots about 25 metres apart. Visitors recorded Moreton Bay figs beside the two registered points on iNaturalist in March and June 2026, so the trees are alive and the area is right. Which crown matches which register sheet is not settled, because several figs grow there, but the size gives the two away. Nobody has published an age or a planting date for either, and we have not found a photograph; readers who visit could supply both.

faq.q: How big are the fig trees at Donnafugata Castle?
faq.a: Sicily's register gives the two largest trunks of 9.5 and 9 metres round and a height of 25 metres. They are Moreton Bay figs, Ficus macrophylla, and stand about 25 metres apart.

faq.q: Do I need a ticket to see the Donnafugata figs?
faq.a: Yes. The castle park is a municipal visit with its own ticket; one source gives 4 EUR for the park only. Hours differ between sources and some list Monday closing, so check with the Comune di Ragusa before going.

faq.q: How far is Donnafugata Castle from Ragusa?
faq.a: About 20 kilometres, in the countryside south-west of the town. The simplest way there is by car.

palermo.intro: Palermo grows one species obsessively. Ficus macrophylla, the Moreton Bay fig, arrived from Australia in the 19th century, filling the city's villas and squares with trees whose aerial roots thicken into trunks of their own. The most famous, in Piazza Marina, is fighting a fungal infection that has cost it half its canopy; its parent thrives in the Botanical Garden. The city's oldest tree is something else, a cypress of about 440 years on Monte Grifone. Around them stand dragon trees, a fig turned into a murdered judge's memorial and a palm avenue inside Italy's first public garden.
palermo.meta_description: Palermo's remarkable trees: a 440-year-old convent cypress, a fungus-fighting giant fig and its 1845 parent, dragon trees and a judge's living memorial.
palermo.question_meta: Palermo's oldest tree is the cypress of San Benedetto on Monte Grifone, cored at 444 years. Why the 1845 fig is the oldest of its figs, and 25 more trees.
palermo.question_answer: Palermo's oldest tree is the cypress of San Benedetto in the convent of Santa Maria di Gesù on Monte Grifone, traditionally called the city's oldest and dated by an increment core at 444 years in 2021. The Orto Botanico's fig, planted in 1845, is the oldest of the city's famous figs and the one with the bigger crown.
palermo.question_context: Two trees get called Palermo's oldest, and they answer different questions. The cypress of San Benedetto, in the grounds of the 15th-century convent of Santa Maria di Gesù, has the oldest date. Balarm reported in 2021 that an increment core put it at 444 years, the Italian Botanical Heritage guide gave about 438 in 2018, and another local site 436; a legend says it grew from Saint Benedict the Moor's stick. It leans against a wall with a broken top, and no dated photograph since 2021 has turned up. The Orto Botanico's Ficus macrophylla, planted in 1845, is the oldest of the city's figs and the best documented, its canopy measured at roughly 3,000 square metres, reportedly the largest of any tree in Europe, held up by 44 secondary trunks. The Piazza Marina fig was grown from a cutting of it in the 1860s and is now fighting a fungal infection. A younger fig outside the home of murdered judge Giovanni Falcone is renewed as a memorial every 23 May.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Palermo?
faq.a: The cypress of San Benedetto at the convent of Santa Maria di Gesù on Monte Grifone, dated by an increment core at 444 years in 2021. The Ficus macrophylla of the Orto Botanico, planted in 1845, is the oldest of the city's figs.

faq.q: Why is the Falcone Tree covered in messages?
faq.a: After the mafia killed anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone in a 1992 car bombing, strangers began taping messages, photographs and poems to the fig tree outside his home on Via Notarbartolo. Palermitans call it l'Albero della Speranza, the Tree of Hope, and the tradition is renewed every 23 May.

faq.q: Is the giant fig tree in Piazza Marina dying?
faq.a: It is seriously ill. A fungal infection has spread through roughly half the tree since 2016, drying out aerial roots and dropping branches in 2016, 2020 and 2024. The city is monitoring and propping it while studying whether it can be saved.

faq.q: Are Palermo's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Most are, in free squares, parks and streets, including the plane on Via Piano dell'Ucciardone and the park of Villa Niscemi. The Orto Botanico and the Villa Tasca grounds charge entry, the Lo Porto nursery is open in business hours, and Villa Malfitano charges only for the house.
